title: The Tower on the Lagoon: a Canon of Warmia Moves the Earth
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Copper Town and the Uncle

stops.name: Torun, the house on the copper street
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested. The house is disputed: English Wikipedia says the house at ul. Kopernika 15/17 'is considered by many historians to be the birthplace', while Polish scholarship (Krzysztof Mikulski) argues for the family's more prestigious house at Rynek Staromiejski 36, demolished in the nineteenth century, and before 1881 ul. Kopernika 40 was the accepted site. Coordinates are the museum house, 53.00922/18.60394.
stops.campa: A son is born in the merchant quarter of Torun to Nicolaus Koppernigk, who trades copper out of Krakow down the Vistula, and to Barbara Watzenrode, of a Torun patrician family. He is the fourth child. The town is a Hanseatic river port inside Royal Prussia, under the Crown of Poland, and speaks German in its counting houses and Latin in its schools. Tradition puts his baptism at the font of St John's, a few streets off; no register entry survives to prove it. Torun historians still disagree about which house was the family's in 1473.
suggested_refs: The Kopernik House museum, ul. Kopernika 15/17, Torun
The baptismal font of the church of St John, Torun

stops.name: Torun, the father dead and the uncle in his place
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day are not recorded and default to 01 January.
stops.campa: The copper merchant dies when his son is ten, and the household passes to Barbara's brother, Lucas Watzenrode the Younger, canon, doctor of canon law, and a man with a career of his own to build. There are four children in the house and a widow, and the uncle takes charge of all of it. Six years later Watzenrode is elected Prince-Bishop of Warmia, sovereign in a small ecclesiastical state on the Baltic. Schooling, a benefice, Italy, and a canon's income for life all follow from that election. No record survives of the boy being asked.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Lucas Watzenrode the Younger, Prince-Bishop of Warmia 1489-1512

stops.name: Wloclawek, the cathedral school on the Vistula
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. MacTutor places about a year of preparatory study here around 1488; no enrolment record names him, and the dossier treats the early schools as proposals rather than documented attendance. Coordinates corrected to Wloclawek Cathedral, 52.661/19.068.
stops.campa: A cathedral school on the Vistula, sixty miles downriver, is where his biographers place him at about fifteen, learning the Latin and the computus that Krakow will expect. The school existed and taught astronomy of a practical kind, and it stood on the road his uncle would have sent him along. That is the whole of the evidence: no enrolment list names him, and the first hard record of any schooling is the Krakow register three years later. Biographers give him a year here regardless.
suggested_refs: Wloclawek Cathedral and its chapter school

stops.name: Krakow, matriculation as Nicolaus Nicolai de Thuronia
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the university register for the winter term 1491/92; the month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: He crosses into the Kingdom of Poland proper and pays his fee at the university, and the register writes him down as Nicolaus Nicolai de Thuronia, Nicolaus son of Nicolaus, of Torun. The fee is paid in full, which the register also troubles to note. The Krakow faculty is then at the height of its mathematical reputation, drawing students from across the empire for astronomy that other universities treat as an ornament of the arts course. His brother Andreas matriculates alongside him. Neither of them will take a degree here.
suggested_refs: The matriculation register of the University of Krakow, winter term 1491/92

stops.name: Krakow, the quadrivium at the Collegium Maius
stops.date_confidence: The course of study is attested for the years 1491-1495; the year given here orders the segment and is not the date of a specific event.
stops.campa: Arithmetic, geometry, optics, cosmography, and the tables that let a man say where a planet will stand next spring. Ptolemy's spheres are taught in this building as the true frame of the world, with the epicycles and the equant that make the numbers come out; the equant is a circle a planet moves around uniformly with respect to a point that is not its centre. He learns it properly, and will spend forty years getting rid of it. He buys books here and keeps them, and they sit in the Jagiellonian collections still, his notes in the margins.
stops.quote: the center of the earth is not the center of the universe
stops.quote_source: Commentariolus, c. 1514, English translation, quoted on encyclopedia.com, 'Nicholas Copernicus'; written some twenty years after these lectures
suggested_refs: The Collegium Maius, University of Krakow
Copernicus's annotated student books in the Jagiellonian collections

stops.name: Lidzbark Warminski, called to the uncle's court
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he left Krakow without a degree for Warmia in 1495; month and day default to 01 January. The canonry itself is dated 20 October 1497 and was taken up by proxy.
stops.campa: Krakow ends without a degree and he goes north to the bishop's castle at Lidzbark Warminski, where his uncle governs Warmia as prince and bishop in one person. Watzenrode puts him forward for a canonry in the Frombork chapter; the first attempt fails, the chapter having a candidate of its own. On the twentieth of October 1497, with the nephew already in Italy, the canonry is secured by proxy while he is at his books in Bologna. It pays him for the next forty-six years.
suggested_refs: The episcopal castle of Lidzbark Warminski (Heilsberg)
The Warmia cathedral chapter's records of the 1497 canonry

segments.name: Italy: Law, Medicine, and the Only Degree

stops.name: Bologna, the German nation of law students
stops.date_confidence: Enrolment date attested; MacTutor and Wikipedia extend the Bologna stay into spring 1501, where the dossier gives 1496-1500.
stops.campa: He enrols in the German nation of law students at Bologna, registered for canon law, which is what the chapter is paying for. He lodges in the house of Domenico Maria Novara, who holds the chair of astronomy and is required by the university to publish a yearly prognostication for the city. The arrangement is not a lodger's: the professor takes him on at the instruments, and the observations they make together turn up years afterward in his own book. Nothing he read in canon law leaves a trace in anything he ever wrote.
suggested_refs: The matriculation rolls of the German nation, University of Bologna
Domenico Maria Novara's annual prognostications for Bologna

stops.name: Bologna, the Moon covers Aldebaran
stops.date_confidence: Attested and dated. The observing site within Bologna is not recorded; the pin is the university quarter.
stops.campa: On the ninth of March the Moon passes in front of Aldebaran, the red eye of the Bull, and the two men time the disappearance together. It is the earliest observation of his that survives with a date attached to it. Ptolemy's lunar theory requires the Moon's apparent size to double between its farthest and nearest points, which no eye has ever seen it do, and an occultation is exactly the event that puts the question. He is twenty-four. Where in the city they stood, and what they said to each other, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The occultation of Aldebaran, 9 March 1497, cited in De revolutionibus

stops.name: Rome, the Jubilee year and the eclipse of November
stops.date_confidence: The Rome visit and the lunar eclipse are attested; MacTutor gives the night as 6 November, Wikipedia as 5-6 November. The lectures on mathematics are reported by Rheticus forty years later, with no venue, no title, and no hearer's account.
stops.campa: The Jubilee brings pilgrims out of every Christian country into Rome, and the young canon spends the year there. He is twenty-seven, holds a canonry and a benefice, and has no degree. Rheticus, long afterward, reports that he lectured on mathematics before a Roman audience; the building is not named and no one who heard him left a word about it. On the night of the fifth of November he observes a lunar eclipse and writes the time down, and that figure turns up forty years later in De revolutionibus.
suggested_refs: Rheticus, Narratio prima (1540), on the Roman lectures
The lunar eclipse of 5-6 November 1500, used in De revolutionibus

stops.name: Frombork, before the chapter, asking for more time
stops.date_confidence: The 1501 return to Warmia and the grant of further leave are attested; month and day default to 01 January. Coordinates corrected to the Frombork cathedral hill, 54.357083/19.681667.
stops.campa: He comes back north to stand before the chapter that has been paying a man it has never seen work, and asks for more leave. They grant it, on the stated ground that he will study medicine and be useful to the canons as a physician. He does not stay long enough for anyone to record what he did in Warmia that summer, or whether he climbed the cathedral hill and looked at the sky he would spend thirty years measuring from it. Then he turns south over the Alps again with the permission in writing.
suggested_refs: The acts of the Warmia cathedral chapter granting leave for study in Italy

stops.name: Padua, medicine at the Palazzo Bo
stops.date_confidence: Studies at Padua run 1501-1503; the year given here orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to Palazzo Bo, 45.4093/11.8762. No Padua medical degree was taken.
stops.campa: Medicine at Padua means Galen and Avicenna read as texts, astrology used as part of diagnosis, and the anatomy the city is beginning to be famous for. He improves his Greek here, enough to translate out of it later. He takes no degree in medicine and never claims one; for the rest of his life he treats bishops and canons on the strength of the training alone, and they send for him from other dioceses. Two years, and no document at the end of them except the chapter's leave running out.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Bo, University of Padua

stops.name: Ferrara, the doctorate in canon law
stops.date_confidence: Date attested; this is his only securely documented degree. The venue is deliberately not Palazzo Paradiso, which housed the university only from 1567; the pin marks the cathedral quarter where doctoral examinations were held in 1503.
stops.campa: He goes to Ferrara for the examination rather than Padua or Bologna, where the fees and the ceremony cost a great deal more, and on the last day of May takes the doctorate in canon law. It is the only degree he ever holds, in the subject he would use least. The old university keeps no single building of its own in 1503; the examination is held in the bishop's precinct beside the cathedral, and the palazzo that later generations point to as the university's seat is not leased for that purpose for another sixty-four years.
suggested_refs: The doctoral records of the University of Ferrara, 31 May 1503

stops.name: Wroclaw, a benefice he may never have seen
stops.date_confidence: The grant document is dated at Padua, 10 January 1503; the benefice was held until 1538. Coordinates corrected to Ostrow Tumski, 51.115444/17.044272. No journey by Copernicus to Wroclaw is documented.
stops.campa: A document drawn up at Padua on the tenth of January gives him a sinecure at the collegiate church of the Holy Cross on the cathedral island at Wroclaw, in Silesia. There is no record that he ever travelled to the city, sang an office in the church, or met the chapter that paid him; the benefice is an income transacted at a distance, of the kind the church of his century settled on men it wanted kept comfortable and free. Two benefices now, and the Warmia chapter still waiting for him. He will hold this one thirty-five years.
suggested_refs: The collegiate church of the Holy Cross and St Bartholomew, Ostrow Tumski, Wroclaw

stops.name: Lidzbark Warminski, physician to the prince-bishop
stops.date_confidence: Residence at Lidzbark runs c. 1503-1510/12; the year given here orders the segment. That the decisive work on the Earth's motion began in these years is a scholarly inference, not a dated event.
stops.campa: For seven years he lives in his uncle's castle as physician, secretary, and diplomatic aide, riding with the bishop to the Prussian diets and drafting his Latin for him. Watzenrode is at war with the Teutonic Order by every means short of an army, and the nephew watches the business of a small state from inside its walls. He observes when the work allows: a handful of dated positions from these years, taken between other men's errands. The thinking that moves the Earth probably starts in this castle, with nothing to date it by.
suggested_refs: The bishop's castle at Lidzbark Warminski, seat of the prince-bishops of Warmia

stops.name: Krakow, Haller prints the letters of Theophylact
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the printing to c. 1509; month and day default to 01 January. The press location within Krakow is approximate.
stops.campa: Johann Haller's press in Krakow prints a small book: the moral, rustic, and amatory letters of Theophylact Simocatta, a seventh-century Byzantine, turned out of Greek into Latin prose by a canon of Warmia and dedicated to his uncle the bishop. The Greek is the Padua Greek, and the dedication pays a debt to the man who bought him the years in Italy; Watzenrode has three years to live. He is thirty-six, and this is the first thing of his ever to reach print. It is not astronomy.
suggested_refs: Theophylacti scolastici Simocatti epistolae morales, rurales et amatoriae, Krakow: Johann Haller, 1509

segments.name: Frombork: the Curia, the Tower, the Little Commentary

stops.name: Frombork, the curia outside the wall
stops.date_confidence: Watzenrode died 29 March 1512; the grant of the external curia is dated to early June 1512. Wikipedia gives permanent settlement at Frombork as 1510 or 1512, so the flat date 1510 sometimes quoted is not reliable. Coordinates corrected to the cathedral hill, 54.357083/19.681667.
stops.campa: Watzenrode dies in March, and the nephew who was raised to be a bishop's man becomes simply a canon of Frombork. In June the chapter grants him a curia, a house outside the cathedral wall, and he takes up residence for good in a fortified brick precinct above the Vistula Lagoon, at the far northern edge of Latin Europe. He is thirty-nine. Everything he writes from here on is written in this place, where the sky is clear perhaps a third of the nights in the year and the sea fog comes up the hill by evening.
stops.quote: the heavens are immense and present the aspect of an infinite magnitude
stops.quote_source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, Book I, English translation, quoted on encyclopedia.com, 'Nicholas Copernicus'; written at Frombork in the decades after 1512
suggested_refs: The Frombork cathedral enclosure and the canons' curiae outside the wall

stops.name: Frombork, the letter about the calendar
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the Fifth Lateran Council's calendar consultation to 1513, not 1514. The Stanford Encyclopedia says only that Copernicus had 'limited involvement' in calendar reform, evidenced by 'a no longer extant letter'; it does not say he judged the reform premature, and that gloss is repeated by biographers without a surviving text behind it.
stops.campa: The Fifth Lateran Council, trying once more at the calendar, which has drifted ten days out of step with the sun, writes to universities and to men with a name for astronomy asking what should be done. Warmia answers. The letter does not survive. Biographers write that he called the reform premature until the length of the year and the month were better known, and no text stands behind that sentence, only the fact of a letter now lost. The correction comes in 1582, thirty-nine years after his death.
suggested_refs: The Fifth Lateran Council's consultation on calendar reform, 1513

stops.name: Frombork, the tower bought within the walls
stops.date_confidence: The 1514 purchase is attested; month and day default to 01 January. Coordinates corrected to the cathedral enclosure, 54.357083/19.681667; the tower stands inside the defensive wall.
stops.campa: He buys a tower in the northwest corner of the chapter's defensive wall and keeps it for the rest of his life. The instruments are wooden and naked-eye, the same ones the Greeks used: a quadrant for altitudes, a triquetrum for angular distances, an armillary sphere for coordinates. More than half of the sixty-odd observations recorded in his own hand are made here, at fifty-four degrees north, where the haze off the lagoon swallows the low stars and the winter nights run long enough to make up for it.
stops.quote: gravity is nothing but a certain natural striving with which parts have been endowed... so that by assembling in the form of a sphere they may join together in their unity
stops.quote_source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, Book I, English translation, quoted on encyclopedia.com, 'Nicholas Copernicus'
suggested_refs: The Copernicus Tower in the northwest corner of the Frombork cathedral enclosure

stops.name: Frombork, the seven postulates
stops.date_confidence: Composition is fixed to 'by 1514' by a Krakow library catalogue dated 1 May 1514 that lists a copy; the date here is that catalogue entry, not a date of writing. The Commentariolus was never printed in his lifetime; the surviving copy was found in Vienna and published in 1878.
stops.campa: A short manuscript goes out to a few friends, unsigned and unprinted, setting down seven postulates: that there is no single centre for all the celestial circles, that the centre of the Earth is the centre of the Moon's orbit and of nothing else, that the Earth turns daily on its axis and travels yearly about the Sun. A library catalogue of the first of May 1514 lists a copy, which is how the date is held down. Nicholas of Cusa had argued a century earlier, out of theology rather than measurement, that the world has no fixed centre and the Earth is not at rest; Copernicus never cites him, and no record puts that book in his hands.
stops.quote: Here, for the sake of brevity, I have thought it desirable to omit the mathematical demonstrations intended for my larger work.
stops.quote_source: Commentariolus (Little Commentary), c. 1514, English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: The Commentariolus, rediscovered in Vienna and published 1878
Nicholas of Cusa, De docta ignorantia (1440), on a universe with no fixed centre
sources: nicholas_of_cusa.journey.json, stop on De docta ignorantia

stops.name: Frombork, the Teutonic raid
stops.date_confidence: The raid is attested to January 1520; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01. That the instruments were destroyed is probable rather than documented.
stops.campa: In January a raiding force of the Teutonic Order burns the town below the cathedral hill and the chapter's buildings with it. The war has been coming since his uncle's time and everyone in Warmia has known it. The canons scatter; the instruments in the tower are lost or broken, and no observation survives from Frombork for the next stretch of years. He goes inland to Olsztyn, where the chapter keeps a castle and its granaries, and his handwriting turns up for the next two years in account books instead of star tables.
suggested_refs: The Polish-Teutonic War of 1519-1521 in Warmia

stops.name: Olsztyn, the register of deserted holdings
stops.date_confidence: The administration runs 1516-1521; month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: As economic administrator of the chapter's estates he rides the villages of the Olsztyn district, writing down who has gone and who has taken over a holding. The register survives in his own hand under the title Locationes mansorum desertorum, and it is the fullest record of his daily life anyone has. Nothing in it concerns the heavens. So many hides deserted; this peasant given a plough team and two years free of rent; this widow left in possession.
suggested_refs: Locationes mansorum desertorum, the Olsztyn settlement register in Copernicus's hand

stops.name: Pieniezno, the second district
stops.date_confidence: The office covering Pieniezno (Mehlsack) is named in the record; the specific journeys there are not itemized. Coordinates corrected to the town, 54.217/20.117. Year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The second district under his administration is Mehlsack, Pieniezno, west of Frombork on the road toward Braniewo. The office is named in the record; the riding is not itemized, though resettling holdings cannot be done from a desk. The chapter's whole income depends on these farms being worked, and the war now starting will empty them faster than he can fill them. It is a small walled town above a ravine, and a canon arrives at it with a clerk, a strongbox, and a list of names.
suggested_refs: The Warmia chapter estates of Allenstein and Mehlsack

stops.name: Olsztyn, the letter to the king
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dossier gives 16 November 1520 for a letter to Sigismund I asking for protection; the text was not reachable for checking in the research pass, and no fetched source confirmed the date. The office and the wartime preparations at Olsztyn are attested.
stops.campa: With the Teutonic army inside Warmia and Braniewo taken, the administrator writes to Sigismund the First of Poland asking for men and for protection of the castle. He lays in provisions, sees to the walls, and keeps the chapter's money where it can be moved at short notice. He is forty-seven years old, a canon in a fortress, doing the arithmetic of grain and powder instead of the arithmetic of Mars. The letter is dated in the biographies; nobody in this pass could put a hand on the text of it.
suggested_refs: The Warmia chapter's wartime correspondence with the Polish crown, 1520
sources: Wikipedia, 'Nicolaus Copernicus' (for the office and the war)

stops.name: Olsztyn, the castle holds
stops.date_confidence: Attested to January 1521; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01. Wikipedia's Olsztyn Castle article states that Copernicus 'organized and led the Polish defense'.
stops.campa: A Teutonic force reaches Olsztyn and the castle does not fall. Copernicus, its administrator, organizes and leads the defence: the walls manned, the gates held, the guns placed, the villagers inside. Command of a fortified place is what the record says he did. Personal generalship in the open field, which later Polish memory likes to give him, is what it does not say. When the war ends he goes to the peace negotiations as a commissioner for Warmia and argues the chapter's losses in the language he took a doctorate in.
stops.quote: what is in accordance with nature produces effects contrary to those resulting from violence
stops.quote_source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, English translation, quoted on encyclopedia.com, 'Nicholas Copernicus'
suggested_refs: Olsztyn Castle and the siege of January 1521

stops.name: Grudziadz, the diet and the bad coin
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the presentation of currency reform proposals at the Diet of Graudenz in 1522; month and day default to 01 January. The Latin treatise Monetae cudendae ratio is dated 1526.
stops.campa: At the Prussian diet in Grudziadz he sets out, in German, what must be done about the coinage. The mints of the Order and of the Prussian towns have been thinning the silver for decades, and the good money has gone out of circulation because nobody spends a coin worth more than its face. Debase the coin and you debase the country. He puts the argument into Latin four years later as Monetae cudendae ratio, for the king and the estates; the principle now carries an Englishman's name. The diet does not act.
suggested_refs: Monetae cudendae ratio (1526), Copernicus's treatise on coinage

stops.name: Frombork, the letter against Werner
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Coordinates corrected to the cathedral hill, 54.357083/19.681667.
stops.campa: Bernard Wapowski, cartographer and canon of Krakow, sends him a tract by the Nuremberg mathematician Johann Werner on the motion of the eighth sphere and asks what he makes of it. The answer runs several pages and is not gentle. Werner has mishandled the ancient observations, and a theory of the precession of the equinoxes built on misdated data is worth nothing, however well the geometry is done. It is the only piece of technical astronomy he lets out of his hands for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: Letter against Werner, to Bernard Wapowski, 3 June 1524

stops.name: Frombork, the housekeeper
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia supports only that 'from at least 1531 until 1539 his relations with Anna Schilling, a live-in housekeeper, were seen as scandalous by two bishops of Warmia who urged him over the years to break off relations'. The often-repeated December 1538 order through intermediaries, and a written promise to comply, are not supported by any source fetched in this pass. Year defaults to the start of the attested span.
stops.campa: Anna Schilling, a woman connected to him by marriage, keeps his household at Frombork. Two successive bishops of Warmia hold the arrangement to be a scandal and press him, over years, to send her away. Nothing survives to say what the household was: no letter between them, no testimony, no proceeding with a verdict at the end of it. What survives is the pressure, and the fact that it took years to work. Later biographers have filled the silence in both directions, as a love story and as an old man's slander.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Bishop Johannes Dantiscus concerning the Frombork household

stops.name: Frombork, the cardinal's letter
stops.date_confidence: The letter's existence and its reproduction at the front of De revolutionibus are solid; the date 1 November 1536 could not be confirmed from any source fetched in this pass, and the Wikipedia article on De revolutionibus, read in full, does not give it. Treat the day as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Nikolaus von Schoenberg, cardinal of Capua, writes from Rome urging him to publish and offering to pay for a fair copy at his own expense. Three years before, in Rome, the humanist and papal secretary Johann Albrecht Widmanstetter had explained the moving Earth to Clement the Seventh and the cardinals and been given a Greek manuscript for the trouble; word had travelled that far. Copernicus keeps the letter, and seven years later it is printed at the front of his own book, before anything he wrote himself.
suggested_refs: Cardinal Nikolaus von Schoenberg's letter, printed in the front matter of De revolutionibus

stops.name: Frombork, one of four names
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia: 'in 1537 he was one of four candidates for the episcopal seat of Warmia, a position that required ordination.' Month and day default to 01 January. The Stanford Encyclopedia, sometimes cited for this, says nothing about it.
stops.campa: Bishop Mauritius Ferber dies and four names go forward for Warmia. His is one of them. The seat goes to Johannes Dantiscus, poet, diplomat, and already coadjutor, which is to say the thing was settled before the names were written down; Dantiscus will spend the next two years writing to him about his housekeeper. There is no record of Copernicus asking for the seat. The office would have required ordination, and at sixty-four, after forty years as a canon, he has never taken priest's orders.
suggested_refs: The 1537 election to the see of Warmia

stops.name: Wroclaw, the benefice given back
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day default to 01 January. Coordinates corrected to Ostrow Tumski, 51.115444/17.044272.
stops.campa: He gives up the Silesian sinecure that was drawn up for him at Padua on the tenth of January 1503, and the collegiate church of the Holy Cross finds another absentee to feed. Thirty-five years of income, and no evidence he ever saw the towers on the cathedral island. He is sixty-five and clearing his affairs down to what he means to keep: the Frombork canonry, the tower in the wall, and a manuscript that has been finished, complete, and unprinted for something like twenty years.
suggested_refs: The 1538 resignation of the Holy Cross canonry, Wroclaw

stops.name: Frombork, Rheticus at the door
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 'In May 1539, Rheticus arrived in Frauenburg (Frombork), where he spent two years with Copernicus.' Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: A Lutheran professor of mathematics from Wittenberg, twenty-five years old, appointed to his chair by Melanchthon, arrives at the gate of a Catholic cathedral chapter in the middle of a confessional war and asks to be taught. Warmia has standing orders against Lutherans. Copernicus takes him in and keeps him two years, and he is the only pupil the record ever gives him. A cardinal and a bishop have already pressed him to publish, and nothing has come of it. Rheticus reads the manuscript, understands it, and begins at once to argue that it has to be printed.
stops.quote: I heard of the fame of Master Nicolaus Copernicus in the northern lands, and although the University of Wittenberg had made me a Public Professor in those arts, nonetheless, I did not think that I should be content until I had learned something more through the instruction of that man. And I also say that I regret neither the financial expenses nor the long journey nor the remaining hardships.
stops.quote_source: Georg Joachim Rheticus, Narratio prima (1540), English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: Rheticus's two years at Frombork, 1539-1541

stops.name: Frombork, the book goes out in another man's hands
stops.date_confidence: The Narratio prima was printed at Gdansk in 1540 and the trigonometric section at Wittenberg in 1542; the year here anchors the pair at Frombork, where the manuscript was and where Copernicus stayed. Month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: Rheticus writes out the system as a letter to his own teacher Johann Schoener and has it printed at Gdansk under the title Narratio prima: the first account of the moving Earth to reach print, and not by the man who thought of it. Two years later the trigonometry is lifted out and printed on its own at Wittenberg. Copernicus lets both go. Tiedemann Giese, bishop of Chelmno and his oldest friend, has been pressing him for years to release the whole of it. He is putting the book into the world in pieces, by other hands, and watching where it lands.
stops.quote: my teacher always had before his eyes the observations of all ages together with his own, assembled in order as in catalogues; then when some conclusion must be drawn or contribution made to the science and its principles, he proceeds from the earliest observations to his own, seeking the mutual relationship which harmonizes them all
stops.quote_source: Georg Joachim Rheticus, Narratio prima (1540), English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: Narratio prima, Gdansk, 1540
De lateribus et angulis triangulorum, Wittenberg, 1542

stops.name: Konigsberg, summoned to the duke
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dossier gives 1541 for the journey to treat Georg von Kunheim at Duke Albrecht's court; no source fetched in this pass confirmed it independently. Month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: Duke Albrecht of Prussia, the last grand master of the Teutonic Order, who dissolved the Order and made himself a Lutheran duke of the same land, asks the Warmia chapter for the loan of its physician. His councillor Georg von Kunheim is ill. The chapter gives permission, and the canon rides to Konigsberg to treat a man in the household of the power his uncle fought and his own castle was besieged by twenty years earlier. Nothing in the record suggests anyone on either side found the errand strange. The patient recovers.
suggested_refs: Duke Albrecht of Prussia's court at Konigsberg
sources: Dossier assertion, not independently confirmed in this pass

stops.name: Frombork, the letter to Paul III
stops.date_confidence: The dedication to Pope Paul III was written last, as the manuscript was prepared for the press; the year here orders the segment and is not a documented date of composition.
stops.campa: The manuscript is done and the preface is written last of all, addressed to the reigning pope, and it is a defence prepared before any attack has been made. He explains why he held the work back for years, names the cardinal and the bishop who pushed him to publish, Nikolaus von Schoenberg and Tiedemann Giese, and deals in advance with men who will quote scripture against a mathematics they have not studied. He says plainly that the delay was his own doing, and that what he feared was being laughed at.
stops.quote: Perhaps there will be babblers who, although completely ignorant of mathematics, nevertheless take it upon themselves to pass judgement on mathematical questions and, badly distorting some passages of Scripture to their purpose, will dare find fault with my undertaking and censure it.
stops.quote_source: Copernicus, dedicatory preface to Pope Paul III, De revolutionibus, English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: The dedication to Pope Paul III, printed after Osiander's unsigned page in the 1543 edition

stops.name: Nuremberg, Petreius sets the type
stops.date_confidence: The 1543 Nuremberg printing by Johannes Petreius, in a run of about 400 copies, is attested; month and day default to 01 January. Copernicus was not present; the object travelling here is his manuscript, carried out of Warmia by Tiedemann Giese.
stops.campa: Giese carries the manuscript toward Nuremberg, where Johannes Petreius prints about four hundred copies. Rheticus, called away to a chair at Leipzig, leaves the proofs with Andreas Osiander, a Lutheran preacher of the city, who writes an unsigned page and sets it in front of the author's own dedication: the hypotheses need not be true, nor even probable, an astronomer needs only numbers that come out right. Nothing on the page says who wrote it. Readers take it for Copernicus for the next seventy years.
stops.quote: Since he [the astronomer] cannot in any way attain to the true causes, he will adopt whatever suppositions enable the motions to be computed correctly...
stops.quote_source: Andreas Osiander, anonymous preface 'To the Reader' inserted into De revolutionibus (1543), cited as 'Revolutions, xvi' in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; not Copernicus's words, and inserted without his knowledge
suggested_refs: The 1543 Nuremberg princeps of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, Johannes Petreius

stops.name: Frombork, the stroke and the last day
stops.date_confidence: The death date is conventional and rests on early tradition rather than a surviving death certificate. The stroke in late 1542 is reconstruction, from Tiedemann Giese's near-contemporary report. Sources contradict each other on the deathbed scene and the contradiction is left standing: the Stanford Encyclopedia states flatly that he 'held a copy of the finished work on his deathbed', while Giese's report describes memory and mental vigour failing for many days before the end. No delivery record and no eyewitness account survives.
stops.campa: He suffers a stroke late in 1542 and is paralysed down one side. The last months go by in the curia below the tower, his memory failing, by Giese's account, for many days before the end. On the twenty-fourth of May a printed copy of the book reaches Frombork, or does not. The story that it was put into his hands, that he woke, saw it, and died, has no eyewitness behind it and no record of the delivery, and it has been told at every anniversary since. He is seventy. Whether the copy came in time is a thing nobody who was in the room ever said.
stops.quote: At the middle of all things lies the sun. As the location of this luminary in the cosmos, that most beautiful temple, would there be any other place or any better place than the centre, from which it can light up everything at the same time? Hence the sun is not inappropriately called by some the lamp of the universe, by others its mind, and by others its ruler.
stops.quote_source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, Book I, ch. 10, English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: Tiedemann Giese's report of Copernicus's last months

stops.name: Frombork Cathedral, buried under the floor
stops.date_confidence: The burial in Frombork Cathedral, near the altar of his canonry, is attested; no date for the funeral survives and the death date is repeated here to hold the sequence. Coordinates 54.357083/19.681667.
stops.campa: They put him under the pavement of the cathedral, near the altar he was responsible for as a canon, with no stone naming him. That is what a canon of Frombork got, and the floor holds a good many of them. The chapter records the vacancy and fills the canonry within weeks. For four and a half centuries nobody can say which body under that pavement is his, while the cathedral is looted, burned, rebuilt, and passed between three states. The book keeps his name; the floor does not.
stops.quote: Through observations made by himself he discovered certain gaps in Ptolemy, and he concluded that the hypotheses established by Ptolemy admit something unsuitable in violation of the axioms of mathematics. He restored the science of the heavenly motions in such a way that nobody before him had a more accurate knowledge of the movements of the heavenly bodies.
stops.quote_source: Tycho Brahe, Opera Omnia, English translation, quoted on MacTutor, 'Copernicus'
suggested_refs: The canons' burials beneath the floor of Frombork Cathedral

stops.name: Rome, nine sentences
stops.date_confidence: Decree date attested. Corrections approved 1620; removal from the Index by Benedict XIV in 1758.
stops.campa: Seventy-three years after it was printed, the Congregation of the Index suspends the book pending correction. Nine sentences are the trouble, the ones that speak of the Earth's motion as a fact about the world rather than as a device for computing tables, which is exactly what the unsigned page in front had promised the reader it was. Corrections are issued in 1620, after which the corrected text may be read under restriction. Benedict the Fourteenth takes it off the list in 1758, two hundred and fifteen years after the printing.
stops.quote_source: Copernicus, dedication to Pope Paul III, De revolutionibus, cited as 'Revolutions, 5' in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
suggested_refs: The decree of the Congregation of the Index, 5 March 1616
The 1620 approved corrections to De revolutionibus

stops.name: Warsaw, Thorvaldsen's bronze
stops.date_confidence: Erected 1828-1830 and unveiled in 1830; month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: Bertel Thorvaldsen's bronze goes up on Krakowskie Przedmiescie in front of the Staszic Palace. The pedestal is cut in two languages, Latin for the learned and Polish for everyone else, and both say the same sentence, that a grateful nation raises this to him; the country doing the thanking has been partitioned off the map for thirty-five years. Copernicus sits above the inscription with a compass in one hand and an armillary sphere in the other, looking past the traffic at nothing in the street.
suggested_refs: The Nicolaus Copernicus Monument, Krakowskie Przedmiescie, Warsaw, by Bertel Thorvaldsen

stops.name: Torun, the astrolabe and the Latin line
stops.date_confidence: Completed 1853; the citizens' committee formed in 1839. Month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: His own town takes fourteen years to raise the money, and the largest single donation comes from the King of Prussia, who rules the town and calls it Thorn. Christian Friedrich Tieck models the figure and the Fischer foundry in Berlin casts it: academic dress, an astrolabe in one hand, the other pointing up. The Latin cut into the pedestal is composed for the occasion by a naturalist in Berlin. Nicolaus Copernicus Thorunensis, terrae motor, solis caelique stator. Mover of the earth, stayer of the sun and the sky.
suggested_refs: The Nicolaus Copernicus Monument, Torun, by Christian Friedrich Tieck, 1853
Alexander von Humboldt's Latin epigram composed for the Torun pedestal, 1853

stops.name: Krakow, Matejko's kneeling astronomer
stops.date_confidence: Painted 1873 for the quadricentennial of the birth; month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: For the four hundredth birthday Jan Matejko paints him on a balcony at night, kneeling among his instruments with his hands open and the compasses set down by his knee, and calls the picture a conversation with God. The citizens of Krakow buy it by subscription and hang it in the university's Collegium Novum, a few streets from the rooms where he learned his mathematics. The library across the park holds the manuscript of De revolutionibus in his own hand, catalogued BJ 10 000, corrections and all.
suggested_refs: Jan Matejko, Astronomer Copernicus, or Conversations with God (1873), Collegium Novum, Krakow
The autograph manuscript of De revolutionibus, Jagiellonian Library, BJ 10 000
sources: Wikipedia, 'Astronomer Copernicus, or Conversations with God'

stops.name: Warsaw, the plaque torn down
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. The statue was removed toward Nysa after the 1944 Uprising and reunveiled in Warsaw on 22 July 1949.
stops.campa: The occupiers have taken the Latin and the Polish off the pedestal and bolted up a plaque in German claiming him for Germany. On the eleventh of February a member of the resistance, Maciej Aleksy Dawidowski, unbolts it in the middle of an occupied city and carries it away. After the Uprising the Germans haul the statue itself off toward Nysa to be melted down, and retreat before it is done. It is back on Krakowskie Przedmiescie in July 1949, on the same pedestal, with the two inscriptions recut.
suggested_refs: The wartime history of the Warsaw Copernicus monument, 1939-1949

stops.name: Uppsala, two hairs in a stolen book
stops.date_confidence: The DNA identification was announced in November 2008; the peer-reviewed paper followed in 2009 (Bogdanowicz et al., PNAS 106: 12279-82). These are two events, not a contradiction. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: A copy of Johannes Stoeffler's Calendarium Romanum Magnum that belonged to him was carried off to Sweden as war booty in the seventeenth century and has sat since in the Museum Gustavianum at Uppsala. Caught in the binding are hairs. In November 2008 the mitochondrial DNA of two of them is matched to a skull and a tooth lifted from under the floor at Frombork three years earlier. No stone at the burial carried his name; the book carried his hair. The peer-reviewed paper follows in PNAS in 2009.
suggested_refs: Copernicus's copy of Stoeffler's Calendarium Romanum Magnum, Museum Gustavianum, Uppsala
Bogdanowicz et al., PNAS 106 (2009): 12279-12282
sources: Bogdanowicz et al., PNAS 106 (2009), read via PubMed Central PMC2718376

stops.name: Frombork Cathedral, the black granite
stops.date_confidence: Sources differ narrowly on the reburial date: news coverage of the ceremony gives 22 May 2010, Wikipedia's Frombork article gives Sunday 23 May 2010, and the ceremony ran across both days. There is no November 2010 date, despite one circulating claim. IUPAC confirmed copernicium on 19 February 2010.
stops.campa: A team under Jerzy Gassowski had opened the pavement in 2005 near the altar of his canonry and found the skull of a man of about seventy. Five years later, the identification made, the bones are carried back into the cathedral and buried under black granite cut with the heliocentric system, six circles round a gilt sun. The pavement is closed over them four hundred and sixty-seven years after it was first closed over them. In February of the same year, on the anniversary of the birth, IUPAC confirms the name of element 112 as copernicium, symbol Cn.
suggested_refs: The 2010 reburial and black granite marker, Frombork Cathedral
Copernicium, element 112, named 19 February 2010
